sources.entry: Cilk: An Efficient Multithreaded Runtime System - Defines work and critical path, proves the work-stealing bound, and shows they alone predict a runtime's speedup.

summary.title: Cilk: An Efficient Multithreaded Runtime System
summary.one_liner: Learn how Cilk's work-stealing scheduler works and how the "work" and "critical-path length" of a multithreaded program predict its runtime.
takeaways: A Cilk computation is a dag of nonblocking threads; work T1 is the one-processor time and critical-path length T-infinity is the infinite-processor time.
Execution time with P processors is bounded below by T1/P and by T-infinity, and the work-stealing scheduler gets close to the sum of these bounds.
Thieves choose victims uniformly at random and steal the shallowest ready thread, which the paper proves keeps critical-path threads progressing.
Programs are written in explicit continuation-passing style: threads spawn children and successors and send values through continuations, so the C runtime stack stays simple.

The authors report that Cilk application performance, such as fib, queens, pfold and ray, is modeled accurately by work and critical-path length, and that fully strict programs get space, time and communication bounds within a constant factor of optimal.
summary.summary: The paper presents Cilk, a C-based multithreaded runtime whose work-stealing scheduler runs on the CM5, Paragon, Sparcstation SMP and Cilk-NOW. It explains the programming model (nonblocking threads, spawn, spawn next, send_argument, closures and continuations) and the scheduler's ready pools and random victim selection. Empirical sections test applications such as fib, queens, pfold and ray. The authors argue that work and critical-path length model performance accurately and prove space, time and communication bounds for fully strict programs.
